lead: This unit explains the machines a clinical laboratory runs on a blood or urine sample: photometers, flame photometers, blood gas analysers and blood cell counters, plus a few advanced instruments — automated biochemical analysers, chromatography and electrophoresis, centrifuges and radioactivity counters. After it you can draw each instrument's block diagram, state the law or principle behind its reading, convert a raw reading into a concentration or a cell count with units, and name the errors that spoil the result.
about: Chapter 3.1 gives the optical core of the laboratory: the Beer–Lambert law, the source–monochromator–cuvette–detector chain, and calibration against a standard. Chapter 3.2 reuses that chain for flame emission and measures sodium and potassium. Chapter 3.3 switches from light to electrodes for pH, pCO₂ and pO₂, and adds acid–base interpretation. Chapter 3.4 counts cells by the Coulter principle. Chapters 3.5 to 3.8 are the advanced chapters: automated biochemical analysers, chromatography and electrophoresis, centrifugation, and radioactivity counting. They show how a sample is prepared, separated and measured at scale. Every chapter after 3.1 reuses its detector, amplifier and calibration ideas.

chapters.idea: A coloured or UV-absorbing solution absorbs light in proportion to its concentration, so measuring the absorbed light gives the concentration through the Beer–Lambert law.
chapters.depth: Electromagnetic spectrum and the two bands a laboratory uses: ultraviolet below 400 nm and visible from about 400 nm to 700 nm. Transmittance T = I/I₀ and absorbance A = log₁₀(I₀/I) = −log₁₀T; A is linear in concentration, T is not. Beer–Lambert law A = ε c l, where ε is the molar absorptivity in L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹, c the concentration in mol/L and l the light path in cm. Block diagram of a single-beam spectrophotometer: source (tungsten-halogen lamp for visible, deuterium lamp for UV), monochromator (prism or diffraction grating), cuvette (glass for visible, quartz for UV), photodetector (photodiode or photomultiplier tube), amplifier, readout. A colorimeter or filter photometer is the same chain with a filter in place of the monochromator, so it works at a few fixed wavelengths; some syllabi call this whole topic photometry or colorimetry. Blank or reference cuvette, calibration curve from standards, linear range, and the deviation from the law at high absorbance. Applications: haemoglobin, bilirubin, glucose, creatinine, total protein. One line on fluorescence spectroscopy, which some syllabi add: the sample is excited at one wavelength and the emitted light is measured at a longer wavelength.

figure.title: Single-beam spectrophotometer
figure.aria: Light from a lamp passes through a monochromator, then through the sample cuvette, and the transmitted light falls on a photodetector whose amplified signal is displayed as absorbance and transmittance.

chapters.example: A 0.20 mmol/L standard of a coloured compound in a 1.00 cm cuvette reads A = 0.30. (a) Find ε. (b) A patient sample in the same cuvette reads A = 0.45; find its concentration. (c) What is the transmittance of the standard? (a) ε = A/(c l) = 0.30/(0.20 × 10⁻³ mol/L × 1.00 cm) = 1500 L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹. (b) c = A/(ε l) = 0.45/(1500 × 1.00) = 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol/L = 0.30 mmol/L. (c) T = 10^(−A) = 10^(−0.30) = 0.50, that is 50 %.
chapters.trap: Forgetting the blank, and mixing up absorbance with transmittance. Doubling the concentration halves T but it does not double A unless the solution is inside the linear range; a glass cuvette in the UV band gives a false high reading because the glass itself absorbs.
chapters.leave: Fluorescence, mass spectrometry and NMR (some syllabi list them) to a dedicated analytical course; glass and reference electrodes to 3.3; the enzyme chemistry of glucose to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: An alkali metal atom excited in a hot flame emits light at its own fixed wavelength, and the intensity of that emitted light measures how much of the metal is present.
chapters.depth: Works only for elements that are easily excited in a flame: sodium, potassium, lithium, calcium, barium. Clinical use: sodium and potassium in serum and urine, and lithium for patients on lithium therapy. Block diagram: capillary tube and nebulizer make a fine spray, the spray enters an air–acetylene or air–LPG flame (about 1700–2000 °C), the atoms are excited and fall back emitting light, a filter or monochromator selects one wavelength — sodium 589 nm, potassium 766 nm, lithium 671 nm — and a photodetector, amplifier and readout follow. This is emission, not absorption: an atomic absorption spectrophotometer (AAS) measures light absorbed from a separate hollow-cathode lamp, and some syllabi ask for the comparison. Calibration with standards, dilution of serum (1:50 or 1:100) to avoid self-absorption, and an internal lithium standard to cancel flame flicker and viscosity differences. Interferences: other ions, flame drift, a blocked capillary, too high a concentration bending the calibration curve.

figure.title: Flame photometer chain
figure.aria: Diluted serum is sprayed into a flame, the light emitted at 589 nm by excited sodium atoms passes through a filter to a photodetector, and the amplified reading is compared with a standard.

chapters.example: A 1:50 diluted serum sample gives a flame photometer reading of 40 units, while a 2.0 mmol/L sodium standard gives 32 units under the same flame. Find the serum sodium concentration. Diluted concentration = 2.0 mmol/L × (40/32) = 2.5 mmol/L. Serum concentration = 2.5 × 50 = 125 mmol/L.
chapters.trap: Leaving out the dilution factor at the end, so the answer looks like 2.5 mmol/L instead of 125 mmol/L. Also remember that the instrument measures emitted light; do not describe it as an absorption measurement.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 for the source–monochromator–detector–readout chain and for the idea of a calibration curve.
chapters.leave: Atomic absorption and atomic emission spectroscopy detail beyond one comparison line; pH, pCO₂ and pO₂ to 3.3.

chapters.idea: Three electrodes in one chamber — a glass pH electrode, a Severinghaus pCO₂ electrode and a Clark pO₂ electrode — give pH, carbon dioxide and oxygen directly, and bicarbonate and base excess are then calculated.
chapters.depth: pH is −log₁₀[H⁺]; normal arterial blood pH is 7.35 to 7.45. Potentiometric measurement with a glass electrode and an Ag/AgCl reference electrode; the Nernst equation E = E⁰ + (2.303RT/nF)·log a gives about 61.5 mV per pH unit at 37 °C. Severinghaus pCO₂ electrode: a pH electrode sits behind a CO₂-permeable membrane in a thin bicarbonate layer; CO₂ diffuses in, changes the pH of the layer, and the pH change is read as pCO₂. Clark pO₂ electrode: polarographic cell with a platinum cathode at about −0.65 V and an Ag/AgCl anode, covered by an oxygen-permeable membrane; oxygen is reduced and the current is proportional to pO₂. Derived values from the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, pH = 6.1 + log₁₀([HCO₃⁻]/(0.03 × pCO₂)), where pCO₂ is in mmHg and [HCO₃⁻] in mmol/L; base excess, total CO₂. Acid–base balance in four patterns: respiratory acidosis, respiratory alkalosis, metabolic acidosis, metabolic alkalosis, with the normal ranges pH 7.35–7.45, pCO₂ 35–45 mmHg, pO₂ 80–100 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 22–26 mmol/L. Intra-arterial blood gas analysers: arterial puncture, heparinised syringe, air bubbles expelled, sample run within minutes or kept on ice, because room air raises pO₂ and lowers pCO₂. Two-point calibration with gas mixtures and quality control sera. Some syllabi call this an ABG (arterial blood gas) analyser.

figure.title: Blood gas analyser electrodes
figure.aria: The arterial sample enters a chamber at 37 °C where three separate electrodes measure pH, pCO₂ and pO₂, and the computer displays these three and calculates bicarbonate and base excess from them.

chapters.example: A blood gas analyser reports pH 7.32, pCO₂ 30 mmHg and HCO₃⁻ 15 mmol/L at 37 °C. Check the bicarbonate value with the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation and classify the acid–base state. pH = 6.1 + log₁₀(15/(0.03 × 30)) = 6.1 + log₁₀(16.7) = 6.1 + 1.22 = 7.32, which agrees. Classification: pH 7.32 is below 7.35, so there is acidaemia; HCO₃⁻ 15 mmol/L is below 22, so the cause is metabolic; pCO₂ 30 mmHg is below 35, so the lungs are compensating. It is a metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation.
chapters.trap: Mixing the units (mmHg and kPa) and forgetting that every electrode measures at 37 °C, so a cool sample gives a falsely low pCO₂ and a falsely high pH. Also, the HCO₃⁻ on the printout is computed, not measured; an error in pCO₂ moves it.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1, electrode theory for glass and reference electrodes, and the Nernst equation; 3.1 for the amplifier and calibration ideas.
chapters.leave: Oxygen saturation and pulse oximetry to Unit 2; ISFET pH sensors to Unit 4; ventilator management of acidosis to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A blood cell is a poor conductor, so when it is pulled through a small aperture it displaces electrolyte and makes a resistance pulse whose count gives the number of cells and whose height gives their size.
chapters.depth: Types of blood cells and typical adult counts: red cells about 4.5–5.5 × 10¹² per litre, white cells 4–11 × 10⁹ per litre, platelets 150–400 × 10⁹ per litre; the five white cell classes are neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils and basophils. Manual counting in a haemocytometer with a Neubauer ruling, after dilution in isotonic diluent, and the dilution and volume factors in the calculation. Coulter principle and Coulter counter: an aperture of about 100 µm in a glass tube, a constant current between two electrodes on either side, a vacuum or mercury manometer pulling the diluted sample through, each cell raising the resistance and giving a voltage pulse of a few millivolts, amplification, threshold discriminators that separate red cell, white cell and platelet pulses by height, and a scaler. Coincidence loss when two cells pass together, so samples are diluted. Automatic recognition and differential counting: flow cytometry with impedance plus optical scatter, where forward scatter gives cell size and side scatter gives internal granularity, and fluorescence or cytochemical staining labels subpopulations; a three-part or five-part white cell differential from the histogram. Semi-automatic and fully automatic counters.

figure.title: Coulter counter
figure.aria: Diluted blood is drawn through a small aperture; each cell crossing it produces a resistance pulse that is amplified, sorted by height into red cell, white cell or platelet thresholds, and then counted and plotted as a size histogram.

chapters.example: A blood sample is diluted 1:500 and 2.0 × 10⁶ pulses are counted while 0.2 mL of the diluted suspension passes the aperture. Find the red cell count. Cells per mL of diluted sample = 2.0 × 10⁶ / 0.2 mL = 1.0 × 10⁷ per mL. Cells per mL of blood = 1.0 × 10⁷ × 500 = 5.0 × 10⁹ per mL. Per litre = 5.0 × 10⁹ × 1000 = 5.0 × 10¹² per litre, which is 5.0 million per µL, a normal red cell count.
chapters.trap: Dropping the dilution factor or the volume actually counted, and forgetting that counts are reported per litre, not per millilitre. Two cells passing together are counted as one, so an over-concentrated sample reads low.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for amplifiers and transducers; 3.1 for the idea of a calibrated readout.
chapters.leave: Flow cytometry optics and fluorescent labels in detail; haemoglobin measurement by photometry stays in 3.1; blood glucose sensing to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: An automated biochemical analyser is a robot that pipettes sample and reagent, incubates, reads absorbance in a flow-through or cuvette photometer, and computes concentration for hundreds of tests an hour using the same Beer–Lambert law as a bench photometer.
chapters.depth: Main blocks: sample and reagent probes with liquid-level sensing, peristaltic or syringe pumps, a reaction rotor or cuvette wheel held at 37 °C, a photometer with a filter wheel (common wavelengths 340, 405, 505, 546, 578 and 600 nm), a wash station, and a computer that stores calibration curves and quality control. Two families: continuous-flow or air-segmented analysers, which push bubbles and streams through tubing, and discrete analysers, which use separate cuvettes and may be random-access (any test on any sample at any time) or batch. End-point assays read a final absorbance; kinetic assays read the change in absorbance per minute, ΔA/min, and suit enzyme tests. Bichromatic measurement subtracts a second wavelength to cancel lipaemia, haemolysis and cuvette dirt. Throughput in tests per hour, sample volumes in µL, reagent carryover and wash. One line on quality control charts for daily checks.

figure.title: Discrete automated analyser
figure.aria: Probes pipette sample and reagent into a cuvette held at 37 °C, a filter photometer reads the absorbance, and the computer converts absorbance to concentration using the stored calibration curve before printing the report.

chapters.example: An automated analyser runs an end-point glucose assay at 505 nm in a 1 cm cuvette. A 5.0 mmol/L calibrator gives A = 0.28 and the patient sample gives A = 0.42. Find the glucose concentration, and the time per test if the analyser runs 600 tests per hour. Concentration = 5.0 mmol/L × (0.42/0.28) = 7.5 mmol/L. Time per test = 3600 s / 600 = 6 s per test.
chapters.trap: Using a single-point calibration outside the linear range, and reading a kinetic assay as if it were an end point. Reagent carryover between samples gives a small false rise in the next result.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 for the Beer–Lambert law, the cuvette photometer and the calibration curve.
chapters.leave: The chemistry of each test (glucose oxidase, Jaffe reaction) and enzyme electrodes to Unit 4; sample separation before analysis to 3.7.

chapters.idea: Chromatography and electrophoresis both separate the molecules of a mixture — chromatography by how each solute divides between a moving phase and a stationary phase, electrophoresis by how fast a charged molecule moves in an electric field.
chapters.depth: Chromatography: mobile phase, stationary phase, retention time, and separation by differential partition or adsorption. Thin-layer and paper chromatography, column chromatography, gas chromatography with a flame ionisation detector, and HPLC with small packed particles, high pressure and a UV absorbance detector at 280 nm for proteins. Applications: glycated haemoglobin, drug levels, urine steroids, amino acids. Electrophoresis: a charged particle in a field E feels a force qE and drifts at a speed set by its charge and its friction, so mobility depends on charge, size and shape; the sign of the charge follows the buffer pH. Types: paper, cellulose acetate for serum proteins and haemoglobin variants, agarose gel for DNA, SDS-PAGE which separates proteins by molecular weight because SDS masks the charge, isoelectric focusing which stops a protein at its isoelectric point, and capillary electrophoresis. Serum protein bands at pH 8.6: albumin, α₁, α₂, β and γ, read by a densitometer.

figure.title: Separation by moving and stationary phase
figure.aria: A mixture is placed on the stationary phase, the mobile phase carries the solutes along at different speeds, and the detector records each solute as a separate peak against time.

chapters.example: Serum protein electrophoresis on cellulose acetate at pH 8.6, total protein 70 g/L. The densitometer reads albumin 60 %, α₁ 4 %, α₂ 9 %, β 12 %, γ 15 %. Find the albumin concentration in g/L. Fractions sum to 100 %, so albumin = 0.60 × 70 g/L = 42 g/L, and γ-globulin = 0.15 × 70 g/L = 10.5 g/L.
chapters.trap: Forgetting that at pH 8.6 serum proteins carry a negative charge and therefore migrate towards the anode, and confusing retention time in chromatography with migration distance in electrophoresis. SDS-PAGE gives molecular weight, not net charge.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 for the UV absorbance detector and the densitometer; 3.7 for preparing a clear serum before the run.
chapters.leave: Mass spectrometry and NMR, which some syllabi list, to a dedicated analytical course; DNA sequence biosensors to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Spinning a tube makes denser particles move outward, and the force that drives them grows with the square of the speed and with the radius, so the same tube gives very different forces on different rotors.
chapters.depth: Relative centrifugal force RCF = 1.118 × 10⁻⁵ × r × (rpm)², with r the radius in cm measured from the spindle to the tube bottom and RCF quoted as a multiple of g; equivalently RCF = ω²r/g with ω in rad/s. Stokes' law settling and the sedimentation coefficient s in Svedberg units, where 1 S = 10⁻¹³ s. Types: bench and microcentrifuge, refrigerated, high-speed, ultracentrifuge; fixed-angle rotors, where the pellet collects on the wall, and swing-out or horizontal buckets, where the pellet collects flat at the bottom. Preparative versus analytical centrifugation; density-gradient separation, for example Ficoll-Hypaque for lymphocytes. Laboratory uses: plasma or serum from whole blood at about 2000–3000 rpm for 10 min, urine sediment for microscopy, blood bank component separation. Safety: balance opposite tubes by weight, close and lock the lid, watch for aerosol and tube breakage.

figure.aria: The curve rises as the square of the rotor speed, so at 4000 rpm a radius of 10 cm gives about 1790 times gravity and at 10 000 rpm about 11 200 times gravity.

chapters.example: A tube is held at a radius of 10 cm in a rotor spinning at 4000 rpm. Find the relative centrifugal force. RCF = 1.118 × 10⁻⁵ × r × (rpm)² = 1.118 × 10⁻⁵ × 10 × (4000)² = 1.118 × 10⁻⁵ × 10 × 1.6 × 10⁷ = 1789, that is about 1790 × g. At 8000 rpm the same tube gives four times this, about 7160 × g.
chapters.trap: Using the tube diameter instead of the radius, and quoting rpm as if it were a force — two rotors at the same rpm give different RCF values. Forgetting to square the speed.
chapters.leave: The biology of the separated fractions; cell counting on the separated blood stays in 3.4; the chemistry run on the separated serum stays in 3.5.

chapters.idea: Ionising radiation is detected either as ion pairs in a gas, which the Geiger–Müller tube turns into one large pulse per event, or as flashes of light in a scintillator, which a photomultiplier turns into a pulse whose height follows the radiation energy.
chapters.depth: Units: activity in becquerel, where 1 Bq = 1 decay per second, and 1 curie = 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Bq; absorbed dose in gray, where 1 Gy = 1 J/kg; equivalent dose in sievert. Geiger–Müller counter: a gas-filled tube, usually argon with a small halogen or alcohol quench, a central anode wire held a few hundred volts positive on the Geiger plateau, one ionising event triggering a full avalanche and a pulse of about 1 V. Every pulse is the same size whatever the radiation energy, so the GM tube counts but cannot identify the isotope. Quenching stops the discharge, and dead time of about 100–200 µs limits high count rates. Scintillation counter: a thallium-activated sodium iodide crystal, NaI(Tl), absorbs a gamma ray and emits light, the photomultiplier tube converts light to electrons and a pulse whose height is proportional to energy, and a multichannel analyser gives the gamma spectrum for isotope identification. Liquid scintillation counting for weak beta emitters such as tritium and carbon-14, with the sample dissolved in the cocktail. Clinical uses: radioimmunoassay with iodine-125, thyroid uptake studies. Safety: lead shielding, time, distance, film or thermoluminescent badges.

figure.title: Two detector chains
figure.aria: Radiation from the sample reaches either a Geiger–Müller tube, which gives one fixed-size pulse per event and is fed to a scaler, or a sodium iodide crystal with a photomultiplier, whose pulse heights are sorted into an energy spectrum.

chapters.example: A Geiger–Müller counter gives 12 000 counts in 5.0 min with a source present and 200 counts in 5.0 min with the source removed. The counting efficiency is 20 %. Find the net count rate and the activity of the source. Net counts = 12 000 − 200 = 11 800 in 300 s, so the net count rate = 11 800/300 = 39.3 counts per second. Activity = 39.3/0.20 = 197 Bq, about 2.0 × 10² Bq.
chapters.trap: Forgetting to subtract the background count, and reporting counts instead of counts per second. Another trap is claiming that the GM pulse height tells you the radiation energy — it does not, only the scintillation counter does that.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 for the photodetector and photomultiplier idea used in the scintillation counter.
chapters.leave: Gamma camera imaging and radionuclide scans to Unit 6 with X-ray equipment; radiotherapy and radiation protection rules to Unit 5 and Unit 6.
